newsitem.title: POLAND: NEW HIGH WATER REACHES OPOLE, DYKES HOLDING.
newsitem.headline: NEW HIGH WATER REACHES OPOLE, DYKES HOLDING.

text.p: A new surge of high water heading north along the Odra river on Thursday reached the southwest Poland city of Opole, where a similar larger swell this month submerged downtown streets.

Disaster control officials said that this time the hastily-repaired dykes seemed to be bearing the strain of the onslaught, caused by new rainfalls over the heavily flooded-south of Poland last weekend.
"The dykes are still holding, but it's hard to say for how long," said Marek Sobczak of Poland's flood crisis committee.
He said Opole's dykes were so softened that volunteers and troops reinforcing the defences had trouble climbing on them.

The Odra surge, a cruel though much less dangerous replay of events in the second week of July, was also bearing down on the badly flood-damaged city of Wroclaw north of Opole on its way towards the German border and the sea.
Sobczak said Wroclaw's residential district of Zacisze was already flooded.
Thousands of Wroclaw's 650,000 people had earlier worked days and nights building sandbag barricades which saved the historic centre from the previous deluge.

But, as in Opole, many Wroclaw districts that had been submerged in more than a metre were still layered in stinking filth that carried a risk of dysentery and salmonella to residents without clean tap water.

Sobczak said an uncontrolled outflow of waters from reservoirs was also sending another high-water swell towards the border town of Slubice facing Germany's Frankfurt across the Odra (Oder) and was likely to arrive in mid-afteroon.
Poland's President Aleksander Kwasniewski told Reuters Television there late on Wednesday that he was sure Slubice and other centres up to Szczecin in the north could be safeguarded.
"I think the most dangerous time was some days ago in the southern part of Poland. We have some fears but we are optimistic," he said.

Apart from the unruly Odra, the vast amounts of water are still covering expanses of south and west Poland and swelling countless streams and rivers tormented hundreds of communities longing for the floods to end so they could start to rebuild.

On Thursday, 2,900 sq kms of Poland were flooded, out of a total 6,090 sq kms affected during the entire catastrophe. The waters still lay over parts of 440 towns and villages, 59 of which were completely flooded.
The total death toll held steady at 55, although there was a likelihood that receding waters would throw up more victims.

Camera images from flooded areas showed people taking boats to feed stranded surviving farm animals, wearing masks to bury heaps of bloated pig carcasses or sitting hopelessly on smashed furniture that represented the lost effort of a lifetime.

Distant weather patterns earlier seemed to menace further dangerous downpours on soaked parts of Poland, but Sobczak said that any rain at the coming weekend was now increasingly likely to fall on the Czech Republic, Hungary and Austria.
"There will be showers at the weekend but this means they will not be intense," he said, adding that there would be greater certainty over weather prospects later on Thursday.

As the government rolled into action with a major reconstruction plan, the billions of dollars worth of damage raised anxieties over effects on Poland's finances, but the zloty currency was stable on the foreign exchange market.
The opposition and the co-ruling Polish Peasant Party kept up calls for September 21 general elections to be postponed because flooded areas were in no state to hold them.
But the ex-communist Democratic Left Alliance (SLD), dominant party in the ruling coalition, opposed the idea and appeared able to block any delay with the support of its ally President Kwasniewski.
